For the SI1000 noise model, the threshold without such a connectivity constraint is obtained in a range 0.23%-0.31%, while it decreases to 0.11%-0.13% with routing, representing a reduction factor of around two to three. Despite this threshold penalty, our resource-footprint analysis shows that routed tile codes require fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than the surface code at sufficiently low physical error rates: Under the SI1000 noise model, we find a crossover near $p^*\approx 0.08\%$, below which routed tile codes become more qubit-efficient, with an advantage that grows monotonically as the physical error rate decreases.

AI.tldr: Tile codes are planar qLDPC codes with weight-6 stabilizers that offer up to 4x the encoding efficiency of surface codes. This work develops an exhaustive search algorithm for SWAP-based routing to implement syndrome extraction with nearest-neighbor interactions on a 2D square lattice. Circuit-level thresholds under SI1000 noise are 0.23%-0.31% without connectivity constraints, dropping to 0.11%-0.13% with routing (a ~2-3x reduction). Despite this penalty, routed tile codes become more qubit-efficient than surface codes below a physical error rate crossover of p* ≈ 0.08%, with growing advantage at lower error rates.
AI.motivation: To improve upon the surface code's encoding efficiency by developing tile code families with weight-6 stabilizers and open boundary conditions, which offer up to 4x higher encoding efficiency (kd²/n), and to realize this advantage under realistic nearest-neighbor connectivity constraints on a 2D square lattice.
AI.method: An exhaustive search algorithm for finding SWAP-based routing schemes that implement syndrome extraction for four tile-code families using only nearest-neighbor interactions on a 2D square lattice. Routed syndrome-extraction circuits are decoded using BP+OSD. The SI1000 noise model is used for threshold estimation.
AI.result: Circuit-level thresholds: 0.23%-0.31% without connectivity constraints, dropping to 0.11%-0.13% with routing (reduction factor of ~2-3). A crossover physical error rate of p* ≈ 0.08% is identified, below which routed tile codes require fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than surface codes, with the advantage growing monotonically as physical error rate decreases.
AI.conclusion: Despite a threshold penalty from routing constraints (reduction factor ~2-3), routed tile codes become more qubit-efficient than surface codes at sufficiently low physical error rates (below p* ≈ 0.08%), making them promising candidates for practical quantum error correction with a favorable resource footprint in the low-error regime.

title: High-Precision Method for Characterizing Degree of Collimation and Beam Quality for Application in Cold Atom Gravimeter System
summary: Highly collimated laser beam with excellent spatial quality is essential for quantum sensing experiments, where even small residual beam divergence can accumulate over distance and introduce significant systematic errors. In this article, we present the design and detailed characterization of a high precision laser beam collimator developed for a cold-atom Gravimeter system, capable of producing an expanded laser beam with a diameter of 16 mm while achieving microradian level collimation accuracy through a five-degree-of-freedom (5-DOF) adjustment mechanism. The beam quality is evaluated using an ISO11146 compliant beam propagation measurement combined with Gaussian beam analysis to extract key parameters, including the beam waist, divergence angle, Rayleigh length, and beam quality factor $M^{2}$. The measured divergence angles of 0.006° (105 micro-radian) along the $x$ axis and 0.007° (122 micro-radian) along the $y$ axis confirm stable and well controlled collimation over long propagation distances. The demonstrated collimation architecture and characterization methodology provide a robust and scalable solution for cold-atom Gravimetry and other precision optical applications that require stable, high quality laser beams maintained over extended distances.

AI.tldr: A high-precision 5-DOF laser beam collimator for cold-atom gravimetry produces a 16 mm expanded beam with microradian-level divergence angles (105–122 μrad) and excellent spatial quality, validated via ISO11146-compliant M² measurement.
AI.motivation: Quantum sensing experiments (e.g., cold-atom gravimeters) require highly collimated laser beams because even small residual divergence accumulates over distance, introducing significant systematic errors.
AI.method: Designed a 5-degree-of-freedom (5-DOF) adjustment mechanism to produce a 16 mm diameter expanded beam; characterized beam quality using ISO11146-compliant propagation measurement and Gaussian beam analysis to extract waist, divergence angle, Rayleigh length, and M² factor.
AI.result: Measured divergence angles of 0.006° (105 μrad) along x-axis and 0.007° (122 μrad) along y-axis, confirming stable, well-controlled collimation over long distances.
AI.conclusion: The collimation architecture and characterization methodology offer a robust, scalable solution for cold-atom gravimetry and other precision optical applications requiring stable, high-quality laser beams over extended distances.

title: Universal quantum cloning beyond noncontextual theory
summary: Quantum theory fundamentally forbids the perfect copying of an arbitrary unknown quantum state, according to a principle known as the no-cloning theorem. Nevertheless, it is possible to construct a deterministic quantum map that produces multiple approximate copies of an unknown quantum state. This task is referred to as universal quantum cloning, further facilitating numerous quantum technologies such as quantum cryptography and quantum communication. In this work, we theoretically verify that the universal quantum cloning cannot be realized within a noncontextual theory, highlighting its intrinsically nonclassical nature. Our verification first {focuses on revealing that} $1\rightarrow2$ cloning scenario {is fully contextual}, and {further covers general examples to observe the contextual behavior of} $N\rightarrow M$ scenario. We believe that our results regarding quantum cloning serve a key role for understanding both quantum foundation and application.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically proves that universal quantum cloning, which is prohibited by the no-cloning theorem but allows approximate copies, cannot be realized within a noncontextual theory, demonstrating its intrinsically nonclassical nature. It shows the 1→2 cloning scenario is fully contextual and extends this to the general N→M scenario.
AI.motivation: To verify that universal quantum cloning cannot be realized within a noncontextual theory, highlighting its intrinsically nonclassical nature and bridging quantum foundations with quantum information applications.
AI.method: Theoretical verification using contextuality frameworks, first analyzing the 1→2 cloning scenario to show it is fully contextual, then extending the analysis to the general N→M cloning scenario.
AI.result: The 1→2 universal quantum cloning scenario is fully contextual, and the N→M scenario also exhibits contextual behavior.
AI.conclusion: Universal quantum cloning is intrinsically nonclassical as it cannot be realized within a noncontextual theory, which has implications for both quantum foundations and quantum technology applications.

title: QUBO Modeling of Module Learning With Errors: Stability and Scaling in Post-Quantum Cryptography
summary: Lattice-based post-quantum cryptography relies on the hardness of the Learning With Errors (LWE) and Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problems. This work introduces a constructive framework for encoding small MLWE instances as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) models suitable for quantum annealing. The formulation jointly represents secret coefficients and explicit error variables within a unified binary optimization structure, enabling their simultaneous recovery from the ground-state solution. Beyond the encoding, we develop a stability analysis of the resulting optimization landscape under additive perturbations. We show that the admissible noise region forms a convex polytope defined by competing candidate secrets, and establish an equivalent characterization in terms of the QUBO energy gap between the optimal and second-best solutions. Numerical experiments on low-dimensional benchmark instances using exact simulation demonstrate correct recovery of both secret and discretized error vectors, and confirm consistency between geometric stability regions and energy-gap behavior. We further quantify the scaling of logical variables and embedding overhead with increasing MLWE dimensions to assess feasibility on quantum annealing architectures. The results establish a systematic connection between MLWE problems and quantum optimization while providing a framework for analyzing robustness properties of QUBO formulations. Although current quantum annealing hardware remains insufficient for cryptographically relevant parameters, the proposed methodology offers a structured basis for studying lattice-based problems in quantum optimization settings without implying a practical threat to standardized post-quantum schemes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for encoding small MLWE (Module Learning With Errors) problems as QUBO (Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization) models suitable for quantum annealing, enabling simultaneous recovery of secret coefficients and error variables. It develops stability analysis showing the admissible noise region forms a convex polytope linked to the QUBO energy gap, with numerical experiments confirming correct recovery on low-dimensional instances. While cryptographically relevant parameters remain infeasible on current quantum hardware, the work establishes a systematic bridge between lattice-based post-quantum cryptography and quantum optimization.
AI.motivation: To bridge lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (specifically LWE/MLWE problems) with quantum annealing by constructing a systematic QUBO formulation, thereby enabling the study of these cryptographic problems in quantum optimization settings and providing a framework for analyzing robustness properties of such formulations.
AI.method: A constructive framework that encodes small MLWE instances as QUBO models by jointly representing secret coefficients and explicit error variables in a unified binary optimization structure. The paper also develops a stability analysis characterizing the admissible noise region as a convex polytope defined by competing candidate secrets, with an equivalent characterization via the QUBO energy gap.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on low-dimensional benchmark instances using exact simulation demonstrate correct recovery of both secret and discretized error vectors. The experiments confirm consistency between geometric stability regions and energy-gap behavior. The paper also quantifies scaling of logical variables and embedding overhead with increasing MLWE dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a systematic connection between MLWE problems and quantum optimization, providing a framework for analyzing robustness. However, current quantum annealing hardware remains insufficient for cryptographically relevant parameters, so this work does not pose a practical threat to standardized post-quantum schemes.

title: Quantum Resources and Performance in the Initialization-Free Bernstein-Vazirani Algorithm
summary: Naseri et al. [Phys. Rev. A 106, 062429 (2022); arXiv:2205.13610] studied which quantum resources in initial states are essential for the probabilistic Bernstein-Vazirani (BV) algorithm, defining its performance as the optimal average success probability over all measurements. In this work, we consider a variant of BV algorithm, which is called the initialization-free (IF) BV algorithm, in which an arbitrary ancilla state as the oracle register is allowed, to improve the performance. We derive an explicit formula for the performance of the probabilistic IF-BV algorithm and obtain a necessary and sufficient condition for an initial state to achieve maximal performance. We further prove that, under a suitable ordering assumption on the coefficients of the initial state, the probabilistic IF-BV algorithm outperforms the standard probabilistic BV algorithm.

AI.tldr: The paper studies an initialization-free (IF) variant of the Bernstein-Vazirani (BV) algorithm, derives an explicit formula for its probabilistic performance, finds necessary and sufficient conditions for maximal performance, and proves it outperforms the standard probabilistic BV algorithm under a coefficient ordering assumption.
AI.motivation: To improve the performance of the probabilistic Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm by allowing arbitrary ancilla states (initialization-free) as the oracle register, and to identify which quantum resources in initial states are essential for achieving maximal performance.
AI.method: The authors derive an explicit formula for the performance of the probabilistic initialization-free BV algorithm and establish a necessary and sufficient condition for initial states to achieve maximal performance, based on the ordering assumption of the coefficients of the initial state.
AI.result: An explicit formula for the performance of the probabilistic IF-BV algorithm is obtained. A necessary and sufficient condition for maximal performance is identified, and it is proven that the IF-BV algorithm outperforms the standard probabilistic BV algorithm under a suitable ordering assumption on the initial state coefficients.
AI.conclusion: The initialization-free variant of the BV algorithm, which relaxes the constraint on the ancilla state, can achieve better performance than the standard probabilistic BV algorithm under certain conditions on the initial state coefficients.

title: Simplified quantum key distribution implementation secure in the presence of state preparation flaws
summary: We present an implementation of a three-state BB84 protocol with time-bin encoding, one decoy state and a simplified measurement scheme that uses passive basis choice. Our system simplifies the state characterization with respect to previous iterations. We also adapt the loss-tolerant method to our protocol, thus dealing with the measured state preparation flaws. We compare the obtained phase error rate and secret key rate when including the state imperfections and when assuming perfect states. Our results highlight the importance of characterization and implementation security.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a three-state BB84 QKD implementation with time-bin encoding, decoy state, passive basis choice, and loss-tolerant analysis, showing that accounting for state imperfections significantly impacts security and key rates.
AI.motivation: To improve practical QKD security by addressing state preparation flaws in a simplified three-state BB84 implementation, moving beyond idealized assumptions.
AI.method: Implemented a three-state BB84 protocol using time-bin encoding with a single decoy state and passive basis choice. Adapted the loss-tolerant method to handle measured state preparation flaws.
AI.result: Comparison of phase error rates and secret key rates between scenarios with and without accounting for state imperfections shows significant differences.
AI.conclusion: Characterization and implementation security are crucial for practical QKD; ignoring state imperfections leads to overly optimistic security estimates.

title: Hybrid quantum floating-point method for sharp arithmetic
summary: There are several possible ways to encode random variables in a quantum state. The basis encoding of bit strings has paramount importance because it allows to load the values of a random variable through the superposition of corresponding basis states, and to then exploit quantum parallelism in processing algorithms. The basis encoding offers a natural way to represent an unsigned integer random variable, and extends to signed integers, as well as to fixed-point and floating-point variables. Each quantum representation of fractional numbers, however, involves a trade-off between accuracy and depth of manipulation circuits. Here, an efficient hybrid quantum-classical representation of quantum floating points is introduced. It combines a quantum register containing the values, with a classical register storing global information about the variable, namely the range and approximation tolerances. The sum and product operations are defined, in such a way as to ensure they are performed without overflow. By taking advantage of the stored classical information, the precision degradation that occurs due to rounding after repeated data manipulations, can be significantly reduced compared to known strategies. Ad hoc examples show up to around $90\%$ reduction in approximation, compared to previous techniques, after repeated additions. The method finds application in many algorithms of practical relevance and constitutes a significant advance in the design of arithmetic circuits with low depth and high accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a hybrid quantum-classical representation for floating-point numbers that combines a quantum register for values with a classical register for range/tolerance information, enabling arithmetic operations without overflow and reducing precision degradation by up to 90% in repeated additions compared to prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum representations of fractional numbers involve trade-offs between accuracy and circuit depth, and precision degrades significantly due to rounding after repeated manipulations. A more efficient representation is needed.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical representation is proposed: a quantum register holds the variable values, while a classical register stores global metadata (range and approximation tolerances). Sum and product operations are defined to prevent overflow, and the classical information is leveraged to reduce rounding-induced precision loss.
AI.result: Ad hoc examples demonstrate up to approximately 90% reduction in approximation error compared to previous techniques after repeated additions.
AI.conclusion: The method significantly advances low-depth, high-accuracy arithmetic circuit design and has practical relevance for many quantum algorithms.

title: SQGen: Structured Quantum Image Generation with Latent-Modulated Quantized Tensor Trains
summary: Generating images directly from quantum systems is an attractive but unresolved goal on NISQ hardware. Existing quantum generators face several coupled obstacles: barren plateaus that block trainability, expensive quantum circuit preparation, and hardware noise that erodes quantum information with depth. A further difficulty is producing image-scale output without a classical decoder, whose use would otherwise break the end-to-end quantum advantage. We propose SQGen, a full quantum generator built on a quantized tensor train (QTT) with a latent modulation architecture. Specifically, SQGen promotes the QTT bond index of the target pixel distribution to ancilla bond qubits, so that each circuit site operates locally on a bond register plus the two physical qubits that carry the row- and column-bit of one image scale. We further introduce latent modulation: each re-uploading rotation is factorized at the angle level into a trainable main path plus an additive latent term, reducing to the trainable main path when the latent term is disabled. During training, we create a differentiable model in the classical system under gate-compatibility constraints, with a torus prior as the latent distribution. After training, every operator maps one-to-one to a native quantum gate, yielding a compact, deployable quantum circuit with no classical decoder in the inference path. Together, these design choices address the obstacles raised above. Extensive experiments on image datasets and synthetic data demonstrate that SQGen trains stably, generates images end-to-end from a shallow circuit with no classical decoder, and shows promising feasibility on real quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: SQGen is a full quantum generator that uses quantized tensor train (QTT) with latent modulation to generate images end-to-end from shallow quantum circuits, addressing barren plateaus, costly circuit preparation, and hardware noise without requiring a classical decoder.
AI.motivation: Generating images directly from quantum systems on NISQ hardware remains unresolved due to barren plateaus, expensive quantum circuit preparation, hardware noise, and the reliance on classical decoders that break end-to-end quantum advantage.
AI.method: SQGen builds on a quantized tensor train (QTT) where the bond index is promoted to ancilla bond qubits, enabling local operations on bond registers plus physical qubits for row/column bits. A latent modulation mechanism factorizes re-uploading rotations into a trainable main path and an additive latent term. Training is done classically under gate-compatibility constraints with a torus prior, then operators map one-to-one to native quantum gates for deployment.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on image datasets and synthetic data show that SQGen trains stably, generates images end-to-end from shallow circuits with no classical decoder, and demonstrates promising feasibility on real quantum hardware.
AI.conclusion: SQGen addresses the key obstacles in quantum image generation on NISQ hardware through its QTT-based architecture and latent modulation, enabling practical end-to-end quantum image generation without classical decoders.

title: Quantization of the classical Mpemba effect
summary: The Mpemba effect refers to the counterintuitive phenomenon that an initially hot system can freeze faster than an initially warm one. Recent years have brought major advances in both classical and quantum realizations, with the asymmetric bistable potential emerging as the paradigmatic classical benchmark because its mechanism is especially transparent and controllable. Yet for precisely this benchmark problem, the impact of quantization remains unexplored. Here we show that quantization shifts Mpemba behavior to qualitatively new regimes, moving it to ultra-cold temperatures that are orders of magnitude lower than those relevant for classical thermal barrier crossing. In addition, quantization produces inverse and double inverse Mpemba effects that are absent in the corresponding classical dynamics. Our results establish quantization as a robust route to quantum-enabled Mpemba effects inaccessible in classical regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that quantization shifts the Mpemba effect to ultra-cold temperatures and produces inverse/double inverse effects absent in classical dynamics, establishing quantization as a robust route to quantum-enabled Mpemba effects.
AI.motivation: To explore how quantization impacts the Mpemba effect (hot freezing faster than warm) in the asymmetric bistable potential benchmark, where classical mechanisms are well-understood but quantum effects remain unexplored.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis comparing classical and quantum dynamics of the asymmetric bistable potential to identify qualitative changes in Mpemba behavior under quantization.
AI.result: Quantization shifts Mpemba behavior to ultra-cold temperatures orders of magnitude below classical thermal barrier crossing regimes, and produces inverse and double inverse Mpemba effects absent in classical dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Quantization provides a robust route to quantum-enabled Mpemba effects that are inaccessible in classical regimes.

title: On stochastic realism and CP bias in diffractive dissociations
summary:
CP bias in proton--antiproton diffractive dissociation can be viewed from several philosophical perspectives, notably stochastic realism and stochastic epistemicism. When combined with the presumption of temporal symmetry, stochastic realism suggests that the laws of physics allow the possibility of thermodynamic antisystems, although whether antisystemic characteristics can be physically realised in nature remains an open question.
  Here, this bias is interpreted as apparent, indicating significant non-unitary contributions and a distinction from fundamental CP violations arising from unitary Hamiltonian dynamics. Such apparent effects may arise from intrinsic stochasticity, from environmental interactions, or from interference between the two. This work investigates the relevant mechanisms and determines conditions for creating, transmitting, or screening a CP bias.
  In the environmental branch, an equilibrated radiation bath may transmit a CP bias from matter-dominated surroundings, although causality constraints may limit this possibility. In the intrinsic branch, the observed bias is consistent with subleading antisystemic effects required by CPT invariance. Further experiments are needed to distinguish between these mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper examines CP bias in proton-antiproton diffractive dissociation, interpreting it as an apparent (not fundamental) effect arising from either intrinsic stochasticity, environmental interactions, or both. It explores conditions for creating, transmitting, or screening such bias, noting that environmental transmission via radiation baths faces causality constraints, while intrinsic effects may reflect subleading antisystemic contributions required by CPT invariance.
AI.motivation: To understand whether CP bias observed in diffractive dissociation is a fundamental violation or an apparent effect, and to determine the physical mechanisms responsible for its generation, transmission, or screening.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis comparing two branches: (1) environmental branch, where an equilibrated radiation bath transmits CP bias from matter-dominated surroundings, and (2) intrinsic branch, where bias arises from subleading antisystemic effects required by CPT invariance. The study also incorporates philosophical perspectives (stochastic realism vs. epistemicism) and considerations of temporal symmetry.
AI.result: The CP bias is likely apparent, with significant non-unitary contributions. Environmental transmission is possible but constrained by causality. Intrinsic bias is consistent with CPT invariance requiring subleading antisystemic effects. Both mechanisms remain viable, requiring further experimental discrimination.
AI.conclusion: CP bias in this context is not necessarily fundamental; apparent effects can arise from stochasticity or environmental interactions. The possibility of thermodynamic antisystems is philosophically plausible under stochastic realism with temporal symmetry, but their physical realization remains unconfirmed. Further experiments are needed to distinguish environmental from intrinsic mechanisms.

title: Using Tanner Spectral Reduction to Improve Multi-Layer Optical Lattice Routing for Hypergraph-Product and Bivariate Bicycle qLDPC Codes
summary: We characterize the Tanner graph spectrum of hypergraph-product (HGP) / lifted-product (LP) codes and bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes, informing qubit routing for three-dimensional reconfigurable qubit architectures. Syndrome-extraction routing depth on HGP/LP Tanner graphs reduces to a single SVD on the base parity-check matrix, using a spectral ratio $β_\text{HGP} = (1 + β_\text{base})/2$ where $β_\text{base} = σ_2(H)/σ_1(H)$ for the base parity-check matrix, and a diameter identity $D_T = 2 D_\text{base}$ where $D_\text{base}$ is the base Tanner graph diameter. Fourier spectral reduction reveals that the BB Tanner graph spectrum equals the union, over the $l \times m$ grid of characters of $\mathbb{Z}_l \times \mathbb{Z}_m$, of the singular values of a single $2 \times 2$ symbol matrix built from the two defining polynomials. This reduces spectral analysis from an $O((lm)^3)$ diagonalization of the $4lm$-node Tanner graph to $lm$ independent $2 \times 2$ SVDs. These results compose into a multi-layer three-dimensional AOL routing protocol with one-time setup cost $T_\text{Valiant} = O(\log N)$ atom rearrangements amortizable over a memory experiment of $R$ rounds. For a Tanner graph chromatic index $χ'$ and $L_\text{layers}$ stacked AOL planes, the per-syndrome-cycle depth is $\lceil χ'/L_\text{layers} \rceil$ AOL pattern activations with no atom motion, an $8\times$ step-count reduction at $L_\text{layers} \geq χ' = 8$. Contingent on multi-layer AOL hardware, this yields an estimated $\sim50-300\times$ per-cycle wall-clock advantage over a single-layer AOD baseline (degrading to $\sim5-100\times$ under AOD-crosstalk overhead), reducing to equality in the single-layer limit. This paper therefore presents a route toward practical routing improvement for future quantum hardware incorporating multi-layer reconfigurable qubit architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes Tanner graph spectra of hypergraph-product (HGP), lifted-product (LP), and bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes to optimize qubit routing in 3D reconfigurable architectures. Key results include spectral ratio formulas, diameter identities, and Fourier-based reduction of BB spectral analysis from O((lm)^3) to lm independent 2×2 SVDs. These compose into a multi-layer AOL routing protocol achieving up to 8× step-count reduction and an estimated ~50–300× wall-clock advantage over single-layer AOD baselines.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient qubit routing for syndrome extraction in quantum error correction, specifically on three-dimensional reconfigurable qubit architectures, by understanding the spectral and graph-theoretic structure of HGP, LP, and BB code Tanner graphs.
AI.method: Spectral graph theory (SVD on base parity-check matrices), Fourier analysis on finite abelian groups (Z_l × Z_m), and composition into a multi-layer AOL (atom-optics lattice) routing protocol with Valiant's routing and chromatic-index-based scheduling.
AI.result: Spectral ratio β_HGP = (1+β_base)/2; diameter identity D_T = 2 D_base; BB Tanner graph spectrum reduces to lm independent 2×2 SVDs; per-cycle depth = ⌈χ'/L_layers⌉; up to 8× step-count reduction; ~50–300× wall-clock advantage over single-layer AOD baseline.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a practical route toward routing improvement for future quantum hardware with multi-layer reconfigurable qubit architectures, with the advantage reducing to equality in the single-layer limit.

title: Coherence Estimation Beyond the Liouvillian Gap in a Finite Nonequilibrium System
comment: Suggestions on references are welcome along with other suggestions or comments
summary: We investigate the estimation of bath-induced coherence in a finite quantum system interacting with thermal reservoirs. Enhancement of coherence estimation is transient and the estimation precision totally disappears at the steady state despite the system retaining finite coherence. By analyzing the full Liouvillian eigenspectrum, we demonstrate that the optimal sensing window emerges from the competition between identifiable contributory modes' temporal relaxation and statistical importance. Neither is the linear inverse scaling of Liouvillian gap with transient optimal time a signature of unimodal contribution to optimal sensing, nor is the existence of multimodal dynamics a signature of nonlinear scaling. The inverse Liouvillian gap does not obey any general scaling with the optimal sensing time of coherence and we prove our numerical results analytically using a general Markovian framework. We further show that coupling the finite system to a quantum cavity and maintaining a thermal bias, transforms the transient metrological optimization into a sustained steady-state resource.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes bath-induced coherence estimation in finite quantum systems with thermal reservoirs, finding that optimal sensing is transient and disappears at steady state despite retained coherence. The authors identify optimal sensing windows through Liouvillian eigenspectrum analysis, disprove universal scaling with Liouvillian gap, and show that cavity coupling with thermal bias can convert transient optimization into steady-state resources.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental limits and mechanisms of bath-induced coherence estimation in open quantum systems, particularly regarding the transient nature of optimal sensing and its scaling properties.
AI.method: Full Liouvillian eigenspectrum analysis, general Markovian framework for analytical proofs, and numerical simulations of a finite quantum system coupled to thermal reservoirs with and without a quantum cavity under thermal bias.
AI.result: Optimal coherence estimation is transient and vanishes at steady state despite finite retained coherence. Linear inverse scaling of Liouvillian gap with optimal time does not indicate unimodal contribution, nor does multimodal dynamics imply nonlinear scaling. No general scaling law relates Liouvillian gap to optimal sensing time. Cavity coupling with thermal bias sustains the metrological resource at steady state.
AI.conclusion: The transient nature of optimal coherence sensing is governed by competing relaxation modes rather than simple gap scaling. Steady-state metrological resources can be achieved through cavity-mediated coupling under thermal bias.

title: Entanglement as a Structural Complexity Axis: A PAC-Bayesian View of Generalization in Quantum Policies and Value Functions
summary: Parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) are increasingly used as policies and value functions in quantum reinforcement learning, yet it remains unclear when and why quantum policies generalize. We give a PAC-Bayesian account in which generalization is governed not by the raw number of circuit parameters, but by the effective dimension of the Fisher geometry induced by the circuit. This quantity is inflated by entanglement, making entangling connectivity an independent axis of complexity.In controlled experiments that fix the number of trainable rotations and vary only entanglement, we find that circuits with larger Fisher effective dimension exhibit larger train-test gaps, while parameter count is a weak predictor. The resulting bound acts primarily as a ranking certificate: it correctly orders circuits with identical parameter count, which parameter-counting bounds cannot do. We validate this mechanism across supervised classification, quantum contextual bandits, and value-function generalization, where entangled circuits consistently generalize worse than non-entangled circuits of equal parameter count, with gaps shrinking as sample size increases.Our strongest evidence comes from low-variance decision models, including single-observable classifiers, value heads, and one-step policies. In end-to-end multi-step policy learning, entanglement effects remain statistically significant but high return variance leaves the full ordering only partially resolved. Partial-correlation analysis shows that Fisher effective dimension screens off entangling pattern, and controls for training accuracy, readout, and optimizer rule out major optimization confounders. The effect also persists on an IBM Heron quantum processor under real noise. Overall, our results reframe quantum policy design around an entanglement--generalization trade-off rather than expressivity alone.

AI.tldr: This paper uses PAC-Bayesian theory to show that generalization in quantum reinforcement learning is governed by the Fisher effective dimension (inflated by entanglement) rather than raw parameter count. Controlled experiments demonstrate that entangled circuits generalize worse than non-entangled ones with equal parameters, establishing an entanglement-generalization trade-off for quantum policy design.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear when and why quantum policies generalize in quantum reinforcement learning, despite the increasing use of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) as policies and value functions.
AI.method: A PAC-Bayesian bound based on Fisher effective dimension (not parameter count) is developed, where entanglement inflates the effective dimension. Controlled experiments fix trainable rotations and vary only entanglement; validation across supervised classification, contextual bandits, and value-function generalization; partial-correlation analysis and controls for optimization confounders; validation on IBM Heron quantum processor under real noise.
AI.result: Circuits with larger Fisher effective dimension exhibit larger train-test gaps; parameter count is a weak predictor. Entangled circuits generalize worse than non-entangled circuits of equal parameter count, with gaps shrinking as sample size increases. Effects are strongest in low-variance decision models; in multi-step policy learning, effects remain significant but ordering is partially resolved due to high return variance.
AI.conclusion: Quantum policy design should be reframed around an entanglement-generalization trade-off rather than expressivity alone.

title: Learning to Reconstruct Wigner Functions in Phase Space
summary: Wigner function learning is a central tool for characterizing continuous variable quantum systems. A fundamental challenge in this setting is to infer a continuous phase-space function from sparse pointwise measurement data, a task that becomes increasingly demanding as the effective dimension enlarges. Here, we develop a general machine learning framework to reconstruct Wigner functions directly as continuous functions from sparse phase-space data. For states with sparse Fock-space or coherent-state representations, such as binomial code states and cat states, we devise provably efficient regression models whose measurement complexity scales only logarithmically with the effective Hilbert-space dimension. For more general states, such as the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, we design a deep learning model that reconstructs the Wigner function from sparse measurements and generalizes to arbitrary phase-space resolution. We demonstrate the broad applicability of our framework on both simulated data and experimental data from a circuit quantum electrodynamic (circuit-QED) system. Interestingly, on experimental data, we find that our model reconstructs Wigner functions of GKP code states across multiple rounds of quantum error correction and identifies the dominant error process using significantly fewer measurements than conventional estimation techniques.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a machine learning framework for reconstructing Wigner functions of continuous variable quantum systems from sparse phase-space measurements, achieving logarithmic scaling in measurement complexity for states with sparse representations and demonstrating strong performance on both simulated and experimental circuit-QED data, including GKP error correction states.
AI.motivation: To overcome the fundamental challenge of inferring continuous phase-space Wigner functions from sparse pointwise measurements, especially as the effective Hilbert-space dimension grows, which is critical for characterizing continuous variable quantum systems.
AI.method: A general machine learning framework with two regimes: (1) provably efficient regression models with logarithmic measurement complexity for states with sparse Fock-space or coherent-state representations (e.g., binomial code states, cat states), and (2) a deep learning model for more general states (e.g., GKP states) that reconstructs Wigner functions from sparse measurements and generalizes to arbitrary phase-space resolution.
AI.result: The framework achieves logarithmic measurement complexity scaling for sparse-representation states; on experimental circuit-QED data, it reconstructs Wigner functions of GKP code states across multiple rounds of quantum error correction and identifies the dominant error process using significantly fewer measurements than conventional estimation techniques.
AI.conclusion: The proposed machine learning approach provides a broadly applicable, measurement-efficient tool for Wigner function reconstruction in continuous variable quantum systems, with particular utility for quantum error correction diagnostics.

title: Epitaxial single T centres in silicon-on-insulator
summary: Spin-photon interfaces based on silicon quantum emitters offer a scalable platform for quantum computing and networking. However, achieving coherent photon emission remains a primary challenge due to stringent material quality requirements. To overcome this, we utilise high-purity molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) to epitaxially incorporate single T centres in silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers. We demonstrate single T-centre emission coupled to a nanophotonic waveguide and observe significant suppression of homogeneous broadening, yielding optical linewidths as narrow as 30 MHz using natural silicon for crystal growth. These results establish epitaxial T centres as a robust foundation for coherent spin-photon interfaces in silicon quantum photonics.

AI.tldr: Epitaxially grown single T centres in silicon-on-insulator wafers via molecular-beam epitaxy achieve coherent photon emission coupled to nanophotonic waveguides, with optical linewidths as narrow as 30 MHz in natural silicon, establishing a robust platform for silicon quantum photonics.
AI.motivation: Spin-photon interfaces based on silicon quantum emitters offer a scalable quantum platform, but achieving coherent photon emission is challenging due to stringent material quality requirements.
AI.method: High-purity molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) is used to epitaxially incorporate single T centres in silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers.
AI.result: Demonstrated single T-centre emission coupled to a nanophotonic waveguide with significant suppression of homogeneous broadening, achieving optical linewidths as narrow as 30 MHz in natural silicon.
AI.conclusion: Epitaxial T centres are established as a robust foundation for coherent spin-photon interfaces in silicon quantum photonics.

title: Calculating strongly correlated ground states from the non-Markovian dissipative dynamics of Gaussian fermions
summary: We introduce a mapping between the ground state of interacting fermionic Hamiltonians and the non-equilibrium steady state of a purely dissipative open quantum system. Within the framework of third quantization, we map the Fermi-Hubbard Hamiltonian onto Lindblad jump operators acting on Majorana fermions. Remarkably, both hopping and interaction terms map onto jump operators that preserve the Gaussianity of Majorana fermions along individual quantum trajectories. As a result, the dynamics can be unravelled and each trajectory can be simulated efficiently using only two-point correlation functions, with a computational cost that scales polynomially with system size. We further show that finite particle number requires negative dissipative rates, leading to an intrinsically non-Markovian dynamics. The corresponding trajectory unravelling involves both positive and negative stochastic weights and exhibits a sign problem and large fluctuations, so that convergence requires an exponentially large number of trajectories. The overall computational cost remains exponential in system size despite the efficient Gaussian representation of individual trajectories, but is crucially dependent on the computational complexity of the non-Markovian unravelling, motivating further studies on the efficiency of such unravellings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a mapping between ground states of interacting fermionic Hamiltonians and non-equilibrium steady states of dissipative open quantum systems, using third quantization to map the Fermi-Hubbard model onto Lindblad jump operators acting on Majorana fermions. While individual trajectories can be simulated efficiently via Gaussian correlation functions, the requirement of negative dissipative rates for finite particle numbers introduces non-Markovian dynamics with a sign problem, ultimately leading to exponential computational cost.
AI.motivation: To establish a formal correspondence between ground states of interacting fermionic systems and non-equilibrium steady states of open quantum systems, potentially enabling new computational approaches for strongly correlated fermionic problems.
AI.method: The authors employ third quantization to map the Fermi-Hubbard Hamiltonian onto Lindblad jump operators for Majorana fermions, unravelling the dynamics into individual quantum trajectories that preserve Gaussianity, described by two-point correlation functions.
AI.result: Hopping and interaction terms map to jump operators preserving Majorana fermion Gaussianity along trajectories. Finite particle numbers require negative dissipative rates, causing non-Markovian dynamics with a sign problem and large fluctuations. The computational cost remains exponential despite efficient Gaussian trajectory representation.
AI.conclusion: The mapping is formally established but computationally challenging; the exponential cost persists due to the sign problem in the non-Markovian unravelling, motivating further research into the efficiency of such unravellings.

title: Quantum Probabilistic Local Differential Privacy: Structural Properties and Sample Complexity Bounds
summary: Differential privacy provides a rigorous framework for quantifying privacy leakage in data analysis, while its quantum extensions have become increasingly relevant with the development of quantum computing and quantum machine learning. In this work, we introduce and study quantum probabilistic local differential privacy, a relaxation of quantum local differential privacy in which the privacy constraint is allowed to fail on a spectral violation event with low probability. This quantity can be interpreted as the probability under the quantum superoperation of a quantum privacy-loss violation, and is closely related to the acceptance probability of the quantum Neyman-Pearson test at a small threshold. We investigate the basic structural properties of this privacy notion and clarify its relationship with existing forms of quantum differential privacy. We show the properties of quantum probabilistic local differential privacy under tensor-product composition and unitary post-processing, while it is in general neither convex nor closed under post-processing by arbitrary quantum channels. We further characterize when depolarizing noise satisfies quantum probabilistic local differential privacy under several representative scenarios. Finally, we connect quantum probabilistic privacy constraints with statistical inference by deriving a lower bound on probabilistically privatized contraction coefficients in terms of the hockey-stick divergence. As an application, we obtain sample complexity bounds of probabilistically privated asymmetric and symmetric quantum hypothesis testing. These results provide a systematic foundation for studying probabilistic privacy guarantees in quantum information processing and their operational consequences for private quantum statistical inference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces and analyzes quantum probabilistic local differential privacy (qPLDP), a relaxation of quantum local differential privacy that allows privacy violations with low probability. It studies structural properties, relationships to existing privacy notions, composition and post-processing behavior, characterization under depolarizing noise, and connections to statistical inference via sample complexity bounds for quantum hypothesis testing.
AI.motivation: With the rise of quantum computing and quantum machine learning, privacy guarantees need to extend into the quantum domain. The authors aim to provide a more flexible privacy framework that relaxes strict quantum differential privacy by allowing a small probability of failure, analogous to classical probabilistic differential privacy.
AI.method: The paper formally defines quantum probabilistic local differential privacy via the probability of a quantum privacy-loss violation under a quantum superoperation, linked to the acceptance probability of a quantum Neyman-Pearson test. It analyzes structural properties, composition, post-processing, and depolarizing noise scenarios. It derives lower bounds on contraction coefficients using hockey-stick divergence and applies these to sample complexity in quantum hypothesis testing.
AI.result: qPLDP is closed under tensor-product composition and unitary post-processing but is neither convex nor closed under arbitrary quantum channel post-processing. Depolarizing noise satisfies qPLDP under specific conditions. A lower bound on probabilistically privatized contraction coefficients via hockey-stick divergence is established, yielding sample complexity bounds for privatized asymmetric and symmetric quantum hypothesis testing.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a systematic foundation for probabilistic privacy guarantees in quantum information processing, clarifying how relaxed privacy constraints trade off with statistical inference capabilities in private quantum hypothesis testing.

title: Attosecond metrology of bright quantum light
summary: Attosecond metrology is the ability to measure ultrafast optical light-wave oscillations, yet its approach has been limited to classical fields. Hence, the influence of the fluctuations of a quantum field on attosecond measurements has remained unexplored. Here, we close this gap by showing that the attosecond streaking measurement of bright quantum light is sensitive to quantum fluctuations of the optical field on the attosecond timescale. The distinct sub-cycle modulations allow to extract the properties of the squeezed field quadrature in regimes where conventional state tomography approaches reach their limitation. With the full quantum optical attosecond streaking scheme developed here, we provide a certification method that can measure quantum squeezing below the shot noise limit, thereby overcoming the problem of tomographically measuring bright quantum light. This opens the way towards quantum optical metrology of field fluctuations with attosecond temporal resolution.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that attosecond streaking can measure quantum fluctuations of bright light fields, enabling detection of squeezed states below the shot noise limit with sub-cycle temporal resolution.
AI.motivation: Previous attosecond metrology was limited to classical fields, leaving the influence of quantum field fluctuations on attosecond measurements unexplored. The authors aim to close this gap.
AI.method: The authors develop a full quantum optical attosecond streaking scheme that is sensitive to sub-cycle quantum fluctuations of the optical field, allowing extraction of squeezed field quadrature properties.
AI.result: The scheme can measure quantum squeezing below the shot noise limit in regimes where conventional state tomography fails, using distinct sub-cycle modulations.
AI.conclusion: This work opens the path toward quantum optical metrology of field fluctuations with attosecond temporal resolution, providing a certification method for bright quantum light.

title: Bosonic quantum error-correcting codes with finite stellar rank
summary: Bosonic quantum error correction (QEC) relies on non-Gaussian bosonic encodings whose preparation cost is a central practical constraint. In this work, we use stellar rank as a resource measure to design and benchmark bosonic codes under finite non-Gaussian resources. For fixed cat and Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) code families, we show that finite stellar rank creates a trade-off among state approximability, energy, and logical protection under photon loss and photon-number dephasing, evaluated with optimal recovery. This trade-off implies that codewords with better ideal error-correction properties need not be optimal once finite-rank preparation constraints are imposed. Going beyond fixed-target codewords, we directly optimize bosonic encodings at fixed stellar rank, revealing noise-adapted code structures and concrete resource thresholds. Grid-like encodings emerge under photon loss, whereas approximately rotation-symmetric encodings arise under dephasing. In the optimized search, stellar rank k=2 suffices to surpass break-even for all dephasing strengths considered, while under photon loss the required rank increases with the loss rate. These results establish stellar rank as an operationally meaningful resource measure for bosonic QEC under practical state-preparation constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper uses stellar rank as a resource measure to analyze bosonic quantum error correction codes under finite non-Gaussian resources, showing that finite-rank constraints create trade-offs among approximability, energy, and logical protection, and that optimizing at fixed stellar rank reveals noise-adapted code structures (grid-like for photon loss, rotation-symmetric for dephasing) with concrete resource thresholds.
AI.motivation: Bosonic quantum error correction relies on non-Gaussian resources whose preparation cost is a key practical constraint, motivating the need for a resource measure to design and benchmark codes under realistic finite non-Gaussian resources.
AI.method: The authors use stellar rank as a resource measure to analyze cat and GKP code families under finite non-Gaussian resources, and directly optimize bosonic encodings at fixed stellar rank to discover noise-adapted code structures.
AI.result: Finite stellar rank creates a trade-off among state approximability, energy, and logical protection. Optimized encodings reveal grid-like structures under photon loss and rotation-symmetric structures under dephasing. Stellar rank k=2 suffices to surpass break-even for all dephasing strengths, while under photon loss the required rank increases with loss rate.
AI.conclusion: Stellar rank is established as an operationally meaningful resource measure for bosonic QEC under practical state-preparation constraints, with concrete resource thresholds identified for different noise channels.

title: Geometric obstructions to quadratic time scaling in multiparameter quantum estimation
summary: Unitary encoding of a single parameter provides quadratic enhancement in precision, with the quantum Fisher information scaling quadratically with the encoding time. However, when estimating multiple parameters simultaneously, this fundamental scaling is not guaranteed. Here, we establish a universal geometric obstruction that dictates when multiparameter quantum metrology fails to achieve simultaneous $t^{-2}$ scaling. By decomposing the Hamiltonian derivatives into components that commute and do not commute with the system Hamiltonian, we prove that linear dependence among the commuting components inevitably generates a slow parameter direction whose Fisher information remains bounded as O$(t^0)$, limiting the overall estimation precision. We demonstrate this mechanism in both discrete- and continuous-variable setups, including collective spin magnetometry and a generalized quantum harmonic oscillator, and contrast it with the Lipkin--Meshkov--Glick model where $t^{-2}$ decay is preserved. Remarkably, while the slow direction fundamentally limits the achievable precision, the measurement incompatibility between fast and slow directions decays as $1/t$, rendering the symmetric logarithmic derivative bound asymptotically saturable. Our framework provides a readily computable diagnostic, given by the Gram matrix of the diagonal generators, for identifying such obstructions in arbitrary multiparameter estimation problems. We further show that the bottleneck can be circumvented by relegating slow directions to nuisance parameters or by employing adaptive quantum control.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a geometric obstruction in multiparameter quantum metrology where linear dependence among commuting components of Hamiltonian derivatives prevents simultaneous t^{-2} scaling for all parameters, though this bottleneck can be circumvented via nuisance parameter relegation or adaptive control.
AI.motivation: While single-parameter quantum metrology achieves quadratic Heisenberg scaling (t^{-2}) in precision, this fundamental scaling is not guaranteed when estimating multiple parameters simultaneously. The authors aim to uncover the fundamental geometric obstruction that limits multiparameter estimation precision.
AI.method: The authors decompose Hamiltonian derivatives into commuting and non-commuting components relative to the system Hamiltonian, proving that linear dependence among commuting components causes a slow parameter direction with Fisher information bounded by O(t^0). They use the Gram matrix of diagonal generators as a diagnostic tool and demonstrate the mechanism in discrete-variable (collective spin magnetometry) and continuous-variable (generalized quantum harmonic oscillator) systems, contrasting with the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model.
AI.result: Linear dependence among commuting Hamiltonian derivative components creates a slow parameter direction with Fisher information O(t^0), preventing simultaneous t^{-2} scaling. Measurement incompatibility between fast and slow directions decays as 1/t, making the symmetric logarithmic derivative bound asymptotically saturable. The Gram matrix of diagonal generators serves as a readily computable diagnostic for identifying obstructions.
AI.conclusion: The geometric obstruction can be circumvented by treating slow directions as nuisance parameters or employing adaptive quantum control, providing practical pathways to restore Heisenberg scaling in multiparameter quantum metrology.

title: Unbiased Estimation of Conditional Covariance for Quantum Optomechanics
summary: Continuous measurements can prepare macroscopic mechanical oscillators in conditional quantum states, but their covariance is difficult to verify. The conventional retrodictive estimator assumes a forward--backward covariance symmetry and can be biased, because physical dynamics such as feedback damping reduces the observability of the state from future records. Here, we derive an exact linear-Gaussian estimator from causal, retrodictive, and smoothed trajectories. For a milligram-scale mirror, it agrees with a Riccati prediction based on parameters fixed independently, while the conventional estimate exhibits a large bias in the covariance-space metric, $d_M \sim 5$. Our method paves the way toward unbiased testing of macroscopic entanglement within a calibrated linear-Gaussian model, which will be applicable to tabletop mirrors as well as gravitational-wave kg-scale test masses.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exact linear-Gaussian estimator for conditional quantum states of macroscopic mechanical oscillators, correcting biases in conventional retrodictive estimators caused by feedback damping. The method shows good agreement with Riccati predictions for a milligram-scale mirror while conventional estimates show large bias ($d_M \sim 5$), paving the way for unbiased macroscopic entanglement testing.
AI.motivation: Continuous measurements can prepare macroscopic mechanical oscillators in conditional quantum states, but their covariance is difficult to verify due to biases in conventional retrodictive estimators.
AI.method: Derivation of an exact linear-Gaussian estimator from causal, retrodictive, and smoothed trajectories, compared against conventional retrodictive estimator and Riccati prediction.
AI.result: For a milligram-scale mirror, the new estimator agrees with Riccati prediction based on independently fixed parameters, while the conventional estimate exhibits a large bias in the covariance-space metric ($d_M \sim 5$).
AI.conclusion: The method paves the way toward unbiased testing of macroscopic entanglement within a calibrated linear-Gaussian model, applicable to tabletop mirrors and gravitational-wave kg-scale test masses.

title: Provable learning separation for predicting time-evolution of quantum many-body systems
summary: Given that quantum computers are naturally suited to simulate the behavior of quantum many-body systems, an immediate question arises: can one formulate physically motivated quantum machine learning (QML) tasks that exhibit learning separations? We address this problem by studying the learnability of quantum many-body dynamics from the perspective of probably approximately correct (PAC)-learning. Concretely, we devise a supervised learning problem where the training set consists of specifications of randomized stabilizer probe states, evolution times sampled uniformly from a polynomially large time interval $[0,T]$, coupled with expectation values of certain observables evaluated on the resulting time-evolved state under an unknown Hamiltonian. For this learning task, we provide an efficient quantum procedure whose training phase learns the underlying Hamiltonian from short-time training samples, and whose deployment phase combines Hamiltonian simulation with the classical shadows protocol to perform inference on a newly given data point. By contrast, the existence of $O(\mathsf{poly}(n))$-time instances ensures classical hardness: by embedding a $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete computation into the polynomially long time-dynamics of a low-intersection variant of the Feynman-Kitaev clock Hamiltonian construction, we show that, for a certain family of input distributions, no randomized classical polynomial-time algorithm can fulfill our learning condition, unless $\mathsf{BQP}\subseteq\mathsf{P/poly}$. Furthermore, we show that the classically hard instance maintains quantum learnability. We also give an interpretation of our results in learning-assisted certified quantum simulation. Taken together, our results demonstrate a rigorous learning separation for a natural ML task based on Hamiltonian evolution, while building connections between quantum learning theory, quantum simulation, and QML.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a rigorous learning separation for a supervised quantum machine learning task based on learning Hamiltonians from time-evolved stabilizer probe states, where an efficient quantum learner exists but classical polynomial-time learners fail unless BQP ⊆ P/poly.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether physically motivated quantum machine learning tasks can exhibit provable learning separations between quantum and classical learners, leveraging the natural advantage of quantum computers in simulating many-body systems.
AI.method: The authors devise a PAC-learning supervised task using randomized stabilizer probe states and time-evolved expectation values under an unknown Hamiltonian. Quantum learning combines Hamiltonian learning from short-time samples with Hamiltonian simulation and classical shadows for inference. Classical hardness is proven by embedding BQP-complete computation into the Feynman-Kitaev clock Hamiltonian dynamics.
AI.result: An efficient quantum procedure exists for the learning task, while no randomized classical polynomial-time algorithm can succeed unless BQP ⊆ P/poly. The classically hard instance remains quantum learnable.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a rigorous learning separation for a natural Hamiltonian evolution-based ML task, bridging quantum learning theory, quantum simulation, and QML, with implications for learning-assisted certified quantum simulation.

title: Typical Entanglement of Superpositions
summary: We investigate universal entanglement properties inherent to superpositions of randomized states. We find that an $m$-fold superposition of typical states may be classified into two distinct entanglement classes via the 2nd Rényi entropy density $s_2$. The maximally entangled regime is defined by $s_2 \sim \ln (2)$, for which superposition adds no additional entanglement. The sub-maximally entangled regime, $s_2<\ln 2$, instead constrains the reduced density matrices of independent components to be orthogonal in the thermodynamic limit, which fixes the entanglement of the superposition to a logarithmic enhancement $ΔS(m)=\ln (m)$. As a consequence, an exponentially large number of superpositions is required to transition from the sub-maximally entangled class to maximal entanglement. We explicitly calculate $s_2$ and the logarithmic enhancement, and demonstrate orthogonality for two canonical examples of the sub-maximally entangled regime (superpositions of pure Gaussian states and of random matrix-product states). We also examine the entanglement of superpositions of random stabilizer states, and discuss their relaxation to the Haar limit.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates entanglement in superpositions of randomized states, classifying them into two regimes via the 2nd Rényi entropy density: maximally entangled (s₂ ~ ln 2) where superposition adds no extra entanglement, and sub-maximally entangled (s₂ < ln 2) where superposition yields a logarithmic entanglement enhancement ΔS(m) = ln(m).
AI.motivation: To understand universal entanglement properties inherent to superpositions of randomized states and classify their entanglement behavior.
AI.method: The authors analyze the 2nd Rényi entropy density s₂ to classify entanglement regimes, derive constraints on reduced density matrices, and analytically calculate s₂ and logarithmic enhancements for canonical examples: superpositions of pure Gaussian states, random matrix-product states, and random stabilizer states.
AI.result: Two distinct entanglement classes are identified: maximally entangled (s₂ ~ ln 2) where superposition adds no extra entanglement, and sub-maximally entangled (s₂ < ln 2) where reduced density matrices of independent components become orthogonal in the thermodynamic limit, yielding a logarithmic entanglement enhancement ΔS(m) = ln(m). An exponentially large number of superpositions is needed to transition from sub-maximally entangled to maximal entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a universal classification scheme for entanglement in superposed randomized states, with explicit verification for Gaussian, matrix-product, and stabilizer states, and discusses relaxation to the Haar limit.

title: Design and Benchmarking of a Quantum Photonic Chip
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)
summary: We present the design and benchmarking of RP000, a quantum photonic processor capable of encoding a quantum system in the degrees of freedom of single photons, based on standard CMOS-compatible manufacturing processes, and working at room temperature. We benchmark it against machine learning tasks, evaluating three quantum-classical architectures of increasing complexity. Our experimental results and simulations show that RP000 achieves higher accuracy than classical networks of comparable size in multiple use cases. Compared to a superconducting quantum processor, RP000 exhibits superior noise tolerance. These findings demonstrate that RP000 can provide a scalable route toward efficient quantum applications.

AI.tldr: RP000 is a CMOS-compatible, room-temperature quantum photonic processor that outperforms classical networks in accuracy and shows better noise tolerance than superconducting processors, offering a scalable path for quantum applications.
AI.motivation: To develop a scalable, room-temperature quantum photonic processor using standard CMOS-compatible manufacturing for practical quantum applications.
AI.method: Design and benchmarking of RP000, a quantum photonic processor based on CMOS-compatible manufacturing that encodes quantum information in photon degrees of freedom at room temperature. Evaluated on three quantum-classical architectures of increasing complexity for machine learning tasks.
AI.result: RP000 achieves higher accuracy than classical networks of comparable size in multiple use cases and exhibits superior noise tolerance compared to a superconducting quantum processor.
AI.conclusion: RP000 provides a scalable route toward efficient quantum applications, achieving higher accuracy than classical networks and superior noise tolerance compared to superconducting quantum processors.

title: Leveraging Metrologically Useful States in Quantum Reservoir Networks
summary: Interest in using quantum computers for the purpose of predicting chaotic partial differential equations (PDEs) has been growing with the advent of newer low-error quantum computers and robust simulation tools. In this paper, we present a method that utilizes a quantum reservoir network (QRN) to predict latent space representations of the high-dimensional chaotic 1-D Kuramoto-Sivashinksy (KS) system. This hybrid approach takes advantage of advancements in classical machine learning (ML) through the use of a classical autoencoder as well as techniques from quantum metrology through the use of a unitary that creates metrologically-useful states. Through rigorous simulation and analysis, we show that the proposed method outperforms alternative QRN implementations without this metrologically-useful state preparation, and also show better performance than classical echo-state networks when weight regularization is not used. Finally, we bring to light potential issues that can arise when using autoencoders within QRC pipelines.

AI.tldr: Uses a quantum reservoir network (QRN) with metrologically-useful state preparation to predict latent space representations of the chaotic 1-D Kuramoto-Sivashinksy system, outperforming alternative QRN and classical echo-state network implementations.
AI.motivation: Growing interest in applying quantum computing to predict chaotic partial differential equations, leveraging advances in low-error quantum computers and robust simulation tools.
AI.method: Hybrid approach combining a classical autoencoder (for dimensionality reduction) with a quantum reservoir network (QRN) that uses a unitary to create metrologically-useful states for predicting latent space representations of the chaotic KS system.
AI.result: Outperforms alternative QRN implementations without metrologically-useful state preparation, and surpasses classical echo-state networks when weight regularization is not used.
AI.conclusion: The metrologically-useful state preparation enhances QRN performance for chaotic PDE prediction, though potential issues with autoencoders in QRC pipelines are identified.

title: Differentially private quantum sensor networks
summary: Quantum sensing is a promising technology capable of demonstrating clear advantage over comparable classical techniques for precise measurement. One application of quantum sensing is in function estimation, which can be done using a network of entangled quantum sensors, allowing for measurements with greater optimal sensitivity than unentangled sensing protocols. In cases where quantum sensor networks will be used to measure data that should remain private (e.g., biomedical data), it is imperative that these protocols include a privacy mechanism to hide sensitive information. In this work, we show that entangled sensor networks are vulnerable to certain privacy-violating attacks. To mitigate these attacks, we introduce secure sensing protocols endowed with differential privacy. We reconcile differential privacy with retaining Heisenberg-limited scaling, and introduce several protocols achieving varying balances between the two. We show that our main protocol, an $n$-node network sensing protocol that injects noise directly into the sensing Hamiltonian, exhibits a tradeoff between the desirable $O(1/n^2)$ Heisenberg scaling of the mean-squared error of the function estimate and the level of privacy attainable. Under assumptions on the network (a common source of randomness and a constant fraction of honest parties), we show that this protocol is locally implementable and achieves $(O(1), δ)$-differential privacy for arbitrarily small $δ$ while retaining Heisenberg scaling of the mean-squared error. We prove that our protocols are resilient to attacks by broad classes of classical and quantum adversaries, and find advantages in the privacy-utility tradeoff when using quantum techniques.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces differentially private quantum sensing protocols for entangled sensor networks that protect against privacy-violating attacks while retaining Heisenberg-limited scaling, achieving a tradeoff between privacy and measurement accuracy.
AI.motivation: Quantum sensor networks used for measuring sensitive data (e.g., biomedical data) lack privacy mechanisms, leaving them vulnerable to privacy-violating attacks. The authors aim to introduce differential privacy into entangled quantum sensing protocols without sacrificing quantum advantages in sensitivity.
AI.method: The authors propose secure sensing protocols that inject noise directly into the sensing Hamiltonian of an n-node network. The protocol assumes a common source of randomness and a constant fraction of honest parties, achieving local implementability with (O(1), δ)-differential privacy for arbitrarily small δ while retaining Heisenberg scaling (O(1/n²)) of mean-squared error.
AI.result: The main protocol achieves a tradeoff between Heisenberg-limited scaling (O(1/n²) MSE) and privacy level. It is resilient to broad classes of classical and quantum adversaries. Quantum techniques show advantages in the privacy-utility tradeoff compared to classical approaches.
AI.conclusion: Differential privacy can be reconciled with Heisenberg-limited quantum sensing. Entangled sensor networks are vulnerable to privacy attacks, but properly designed quantum protocols with noise injection can provide strong privacy guarantees while maintaining quantum-enhanced measurement precision.

title: Continuous Narrow-Linewidth Superradiance in Waveguide QED
summary: Superradiant lasers promise continuous, narrow-linewidth coherent emission at the bare atomic transition frequency, enabling frequency references of exceptional precision. Recent experiments have advanced the field, but achieving truly continuous operation remains technically challenging. Here we propose an alternative route to an active optical frequency reference with fewer emitters using all-to-all dipole-dipole interactions mediated by a nanophotonic waveguide. We show that selectively pumping only a sub-ensemble of emitters, rather than the full ensemble, substantially improves emission characteristics. The collective interactions with unpumped emitters provide narrowband frequency selection and establish an effective feedback mechanism analogous to the role of a macroscopic cavity. We find directional superradiant emission with strongly phase-synchronized emitter correlations and a narrow output spectrum close to the bare emitter resonance. Our results demonstrate a strong metrological gain from selective partial pumping of quantum emitters with the second-order intensity correlation $g^{(2)}(0)\simeq 1$, indicating reduced equal-time intensity fluctuations, and open a route to waveguide-based optical frequency references using small clock-atom ensembles for chip-scale precision metrology.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a waveguide-based superradiant laser using selective partial pumping of quantum emitters to achieve narrow-linewidth, continuous coherent emission without a macroscopic cavity, enabling chip-scale optical frequency references.
AI.motivation: Superradiant lasers promise continuous narrow-linewidth emission at atomic transition frequencies for precision frequency references, but achieving truly continuous operation remains technically challenging.
AI.method: The authors propose using all-to-all dipole-dipole interactions mediated by a nanophotonic waveguide with selective pumping of only a sub-ensemble of emitters, where unpumped emitters provide narrowband frequency selection and effective feedback analogous to a macroscopic cavity.
AI.result: Directional superradiant emission with strongly phase-synchronized emitter correlations, narrow output spectrum near the bare emitter resonance, and second-order intensity correlation g^(2)(0) ≈ 1 indicating reduced equal-time intensity fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: Selective partial pumping yields strong metrological gain and opens a route to waveguide-based optical frequency references using small clock-atom ensembles for chip-scale precision metrology.

title: Quantum Channel Polynomial Processing
summary: We introduce a quantum algorithmic framework based on probabilistic mixtures of unitary channels that, similar to the framework of quantum singular value transformations, enables the application of arbitrary polynomials of hermitian operators onto arbitrary initial states. We show that our framework supports a flexible tradeoff between sample- and query complexity ranging from optimal query complexity, meaning logarithmic in the error, and exponentially scaling sample complexity to sub-polynomial query complexity in the error and polynomial sample complexity. Combined with the considerably lower quantum circuit complexity, compared to quantum singular value transformations with a linear combination of unitaries block encoding, we argue that our framework can be seamlessly scaled from NISQ to fault-tolerant quantum computing.

AI.tldr: Introduces a quantum algorithmic framework using probabilistic mixtures of unitary channels that applies arbitrary polynomials of Hermitian operators to initial states, with flexible tradeoffs between sample and query complexity, and lower circuit complexity suitable from NISQ to fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum algorithmic framework that supports flexible tradeoffs between sample and query complexity while having lower quantum circuit complexity compared to existing methods like quantum singular value transformations, enabling scalability from NISQ to fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.method: Probabilistic mixtures of unitary channels as an alternative to quantum singular value transformations with linear combination of unitaries (LCU) block encoding.
AI.result: The framework supports a flexible tradeoff: optimal query complexity (logarithmic in error) with exponentially scaling sample complexity, or sub-polynomial query complexity with polynomial sample complexity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework has considerably lower quantum circuit complexity than QSVT with LCU block encoding and can be seamlessly scaled from NISQ to fault-tolerant quantum computing.
